damaging_scenes.scene: Half-Blood Prince - Dumbledore arrives at Privet Drive / Dursley visit
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book establishes a lengthy, characterful visit where Dumbledore commands the Dursleys with playful authority: conjuring mead that nudges them, finishing Vernon's sentences, making dry remarks about their rudeness, delivering a firm moral rebuke about Harry's treatment, and discussing Sirius's will, Kreacher, and Buckbeak. He is witty, warm, subtly threatening, and fully in control. This extended scene establishes Dumbledore's personality and his genuine care for Harry before their journey.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film entirely omits the Dursley visit and the formal collection of Harry from Privet Drive. Dumbledore instead appears on a London train platform, says only a few lines, and Apparates Harry directly to the Burrow. There is no Dursley confrontation, no mead, no moral rebuke, no Sirius's will discussion, no Kreacher resolution, and no private broom-shed conversation with Harry about Sirius's death, the prophecy, or the upcoming private lessons.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The Dursley visit is one of Dumbledore's richest characterisation scenes in the entire series: it shows his playful command, his moral authority, his dry wit, his genuine tenderness toward Harry, and his ability to be simultaneously disarming and formidable. Its total absence removes a defining portrait of who Dumbledore is outside Hogwarts, and strips Harry of the emotionally important private conversation in the broom shed about Sirius and the prophecy.

damaging_scenes.book_baseline: After the Dursley visit, Dumbledore takes Harry aside in the Weasleys' broom shed and explicitly acknowledges Harry's grief over Sirius with compassion and specificity ('It was cruel that you and Sirius had such a short time together'). He praises Harry's resilience, advises him to share the prophecy with Ron and Hermione, announces the private lessons, and instructs Harry to keep his Invisibility Cloak at all times. This scene establishes Dumbledore's emotional attentiveness and the mentoring framework for the entire year.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The broom shed scene does not exist in the film. None of its content — the acknowledgement of Harry's grief, the praise, the instruction to share the prophecy, the announcement of lessons — is conveyed in any equivalent scene.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is the scene that establishes the emotional core of the Dumbledore–Harry relationship for the sixth book: mutual trust, Dumbledore's attentiveness to Harry's inner life, and the framework of the private lessons as deliberate preparation. Its absence means the film's version of their mentoring relationship begins without this emotional foundation, weakening the resonance of Dumbledore's death.

damaging_scenes.scene: Half-Blood Prince - First private lesson (Pensieve session on Gaunt family / Bob Ogden memory)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book's first formal private lesson is a rich, extended Pensieve session covering the Gaunt family, Voldemort's heritage, Merope's love potion, and Tom Riddle Sr. Dumbledore contextualises everything carefully, makes observations about Voldemort's psychology, and creates a sustained pedagogical relationship with Harry. Multiple lessons follow, each adding layers.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film compresses the entire arc of Pensieve lessons drastically. The Gaunt family memory, Bob Ogden's visit, Morfin's memory, Hepzibah Smith's memory, and Dumbledore's own memory of the adult Voldemort requesting the teaching post are all absent. The film essentially shows only two Pensieve scenes: young Tom Riddle at the orphanage and the Slughorn Horcrux memory.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The private lessons are Dumbledore's primary narrative function in Half-Blood Prince: he is systematically equipping Harry with knowledge of Voldemort's past to enable the Horcrux hunt. Removing the majority of these lessons removes most of Dumbledore's active agency as a teacher and strategist, reducing him from a methodical architect of Harry's preparation to a character who mostly delivers exposition about Slughorn and then dies.

damaging_scenes.scene: Half-Blood Prince - Dumbledore's post-lesson discussions and explanations
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: After each Pensieve session, Dumbledore engages Harry in extended discussion: drawing attention to Riddle's trophy-collecting, his self-sufficiency, his contempt for the name Tom, his attachment to Hogwarts, his Horcrux theory, the significance of the diary, the ring, the locket, Hufflepuff's cup, Nagini, and the sixth unknown Horcrux. He also explicitly discusses his own fallibility and mistakes, and shares his reasoning about Voldemort's psychology at length. These conversations establish Dumbledore as a thinker and a humble, self-aware figure.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film's equivalent of this material is heavily compressed into a single post-Pensieve scene (scene 30 in the film corpus) where Dumbledore reacts to the Slughorn memory and briefly explains Horcruxes. The careful analytical discussions, the enumeration of likely Horcruxes, the discussion of the diary, the ring and how it was found, the humility about his own mistakes, and the extended conversation about love as Harry's power are all absent or drastically truncated.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Dumbledore's analytical, discursive voice — his habit of thinking aloud, making connections, acknowledging uncertainty, and treating Harry as an intellectual partner — is a defining character trait. The film reduces these exchanges to functional plot delivery, stripping Dumbledore of much of his distinctive intellectual personality.

damaging_scenes.scene: Half-Blood Prince - Dumbledore's 'haunted' reaction to the Slughorn memory (film scene 30)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, after viewing the true Slughorn memory, Dumbledore is measured and analytical. He says 'I have been hoping for this piece of evidence for a very long time. It confirms the theory on which I have been working.' He proceeds to explain Horcrux theory carefully, discusses how many Horcruxes Voldemort likely made, and engages Harry as a thinking partner. He is calm, purposeful, and in command.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In film scene 30, Dumbledore reacts to the memory with visible distress: 'This is beyond anything I imagined... I know now... you will see worse.' He appears shaken and emotionally destabilised, staring into the distance. This is a fundamentally different register — not the controlled, long-prepared strategist of the book, but a figure caught off-guard and overwhelmed.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's Dumbledore has long suspected and prepared for this revelation; his reaction is that of a man whose theory is confirmed, not one who is shocked. The film's version makes him seem to have underestimated Voldemort, which undermines his characterisation as an omniscient and strategically far-sighted figure and misrepresents the emotional logic of the scene.

damaging_scenes.scene: Half-Blood Prince - Dumbledore's confrontation with Scrimgeour (Christmas at the Burrow)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book establishes through Harry's conversation with Scrimgeour that Dumbledore has actively intervened to protect Harry from Ministry pressure all year, and that he and Scrimgeour have a frosty, adversarial relationship over the Ministry's approach. Dumbledore is shown as a political operator who understands power and chooses his battles carefully. When Harry reports back 'Dumbledore's man through and through,' Dumbledore is visibly moved and responds with genuine warmth and dignity.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The Scrimgeour subplot is entirely absent from the film. There is no Ministry pressure on Harry, no Scrimgeour visit, and no moment where Harry declares himself Dumbledore's man and Dumbledore is moved by it.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The Scrimgeour scenes establish Dumbledore as a politically astute figure who shields Harry, and the 'Dumbledore's man through and through' exchange is a quietly important moment of mutual loyalty. Its absence loses a dimension of Dumbledore as a figure who operates strategically beyond Hogwarts walls.

damaging_scenes.scene: Half-Blood Prince - Snape/Dumbledore argument on Astronomy Tower (film scene 32)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book does not contain this scene. In the books, Hagrid overhears Dumbledore telling Snape he agreed to do something and Snape expressing reluctance — which Harry interprets as Dumbledore forcing Snape to investigate Malfoy. There is no direct confrontation depicted between them.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film scene 32 shows Harry eavesdropping on Snape telling Dumbledore he doesn't want to do 'this' anymore and asking if Dumbledore has considered that he takes too much for granted, with Dumbledore responding crisply that Snape agreed and there is nothing more to discuss. This is depicted as a tense power confrontation.
damaging_scenes.explanation: While this scene is drawn from a book reference (Hagrid's overheard conversation), dramatising it directly as an open confrontation changes the dynamic between Dumbledore and Snape. The book keeps their arrangement opaque and trusting; the film makes it appear as a coercive command relationship, which subtly alters how Dumbledore's trust in Snape reads and anticipates the Unbreakable Vow revelation in a way that is not present in the source.

damaging_scenes.scene: Half-Blood Prince - Astronomy Tower scene: Dumbledore immobilises Harry (omitted)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Dumbledore wordlessly immobilises Harry under the Invisibility Cloak before Malfoy arrives, making a deliberate choice to protect Harry at the cost of his own ability to defend himself. This act of self-sacrifice — Dumbledore's last active choice — is a profound moment that underlines his priorities. Harry understands immediately after Dumbledore's death that 'the second he had taken to perform the spell had cost him the chance of defending himself.'
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film, Dumbledore instead verbally instructs Harry to hide below the tower through the lattice floor, and Harry obeys voluntarily. There is no wordless Body-Bind spell, no sacrifice of defensive capability, and no moment of Dumbledore actively choosing Harry's safety over his own survival.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The wordless immobilisation is Dumbledore's last major active choice in the narrative, and it is a crucial act of self-sacrifice that defines his character. By replacing it with a verbal instruction that Harry follows willingly, the film removes Dumbledore's agency in that final moment and loses the thematic resonance of him choosing Harry's life over his own defence. This is a significant structural loss.

damaging_scenes.scene: Half-Blood Prince - Astronomy Tower: Dumbledore's extended dialogue with Malfoy
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Dumbledore engages Malfoy in a lengthy, patient, and strategically compassionate conversation: he identifies each of Malfoy's attempts on his life ('these are feeble attempts'), acknowledges that he has been protecting Malfoy all year by not confronting him, explains the situation to Malfoy ('I knew that you would have been murdered'), and explicitly offers him sanctuary for himself and his mother. He also draws Malfoy close to lowering his wand through a careful appeal to his humanity. The Death Eaters then arrive and Dumbledore continues to face them with composure.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film covers similar ground but compresses it considerably. Dumbledore still identifies the attempts and questions whether Malfoy's heart is in it. However, the extended sequence in which Dumbledore explicitly tells Malfoy he has been protecting him all year, explains his reasoning about not confronting him earlier, and offers specific sanctuary ('Come over to the right side, Draco... I can send members of the Order to your mother tonight') is significantly shortened. Key lines about Dumbledore's deliberate protection of Malfoy are absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's Tower scene is Dumbledore's most explicit statement of his philosophy of mercy and his long-game strategy of protecting even those who threaten him. The compression loses some of the full articulation of why Dumbledore is the figure he is. The film retains enough to be broadly faithful but loses important nuance about his proactive protection of Malfoy.

damaging_scenes.scene: Half-Blood Prince - Cave scene: 'I am not worried, Harry. I am with you' (cut from theatrical release)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: As Harry and Dumbledore swim out of the cave, Harry reassures a weakened Dumbledore that it will be all right. Dumbledore responds: 'I am not worried, Harry. I am with you.' This line is the emotional pinnacle of their relationship — Dumbledore expressing complete trust in Harry, reversing the usual dynamic of the powerful protecting the young.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Per the non-theatrical exclusions, the scene where Dumbledore says 'I am not worried, Harry. I am with you' on leaving the cave was cut from the theatrical release. The line does not appear in the film.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This line is one of the most important expressions of the Dumbledore–Harry relationship in the entire saga: it shows Dumbledore's trust in Harry as a person rather than merely a weapon or protégé, and it inverts the protective dynamic in a way that carries enormous emotional weight. Its loss is a meaningful reduction in the relationship's depth as portrayed on screen.

damaging_scenes.scene: Half-Blood Prince - Dumbledore's death and immediate aftermath: funeral
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book includes Dumbledore's funeral as a rich, extended scene: merpeople singing, centaurs watching from the forest, Hagrid carrying the body, the white tomb forming from flames, Scrimgeour attempting to press Harry immediately after, and Harry's private grief and decision-making. The funeral establishes the full weight of Dumbledore's significance to the world and to Harry.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film omits Dumbledore's funeral entirely. After the wand-raising salute in the courtyard, the film cuts to the Astronomy Tower the following day with Harry, Hermione, Ron and Ginny discussing the fake Horcrux. There is no funeral scene, no white tomb, no gathering of the wizarding world, no Scrimgeour confrontation, and no formal farewell.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The funeral is the narrative seal on Dumbledore's arc and the moment that crystallises Harry's resolve and grief. Its absence means the film does not properly close Dumbledore's story or give the audience — or Harry — a formal moment of mourning. The emotional transition from his death to Harry's determination to continue the mission loses its structural anchor.

damaging_scenes.scene: Half-Blood Prince - Harry's confrontation with Dumbledore about Snape and Trelawney's revelation
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Harry discovers from Trelawney that it was Snape who overheard the prophecy and conveyed it to Voldemort. He races to Dumbledore in a fury, shouting accusations. Dumbledore listens and then delivers a careful, measured defence of Snape's remorse and his own reasons for trusting him, while acknowledging the gravity of Snape's original act. He also tells Harry they must go, choosing to take Harry even while Harry is in a rage. This exchange is important for establishing Dumbledore's unshakeable faith in Snape and his ability to hold complex moral positions.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The Trelawney revelation about Snape and the prophecy does not occur in the film. Harry does not confront Dumbledore about Snape before they leave for the cave. The entire dynamic of Dumbledore defending Snape while Harry rages is absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This confrontation is the last major conversation between Harry and Dumbledore and it establishes Dumbledore's unwavering trust in Snape as a conscious, informed choice rather than naivety. Its absence means the audience does not see Dumbledore make a clear-eyed defence of Snape in the moments before his death, which matters for understanding the full weight of 'Severus... please' on the tower and for the eventual revelation in Deathly Hallows.

damaging_scenes.scene: Half-Blood Prince - Dumbledore's office scene establishing private lesson framework and prophecy discussion
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book's first formal private lesson includes Dumbledore explicitly telling Harry that he has decided to take a greater hand in his education, discussing the prophecy as the framework for everything, inviting Harry to share the prophecy content with Ron and Hermione, and explaining the lessons' purpose. He is forthcoming, treats Harry as a partner in a shared mission, and is explicitly humble about the limits of his own knowledge ('I may be as woefully wrong as Humphrey Belcher').
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film scene 18 (Dumbledore's office after the orphanage Pensieve) shows Dumbledore explaining that Slughorn possesses something he desires, that Harry should let Slughorn collect him, and that he will explain in time. The framework of the lessons is not explicitly established, the prophecy is not discussed, and Dumbledore's explicit invitation to Harry as a partner in reasoning is absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book carefully establishes that Dumbledore is treating Harry as a participant in a shared intellectual and strategic enterprise, not simply deploying him as a tool against Slughorn. The film version leaves the relationship more opaque and instrumental, reducing Harry to an asset Dumbledore is using to extract information rather than a student he is deliberately preparing.

main_damage_causes: Wholesale removal of the private lesson arc: the majority of Dumbledore's Pensieve sessions, post-session discussions, and the careful pedagogical relationship they establish are cut, eliminating most of Dumbledore's active narrative function in the film and reducing him from a methodical architect of Harry's preparation to a largely reactive figure who dies before completing his work

Loss of key relationship-defining moments — the Dursley visit, the broom-shed conversation, the cave exit line, and the pre-cave confrontation about Snape — which together establish the emotional depth and mutual trust of the Dumbledore–Harry bond, making his death feel less structurally earned

Omission of Dumbledore's last active agency (the wordless immobilisation of Harry) and the funeral scene, which together remove both his final self-sacrificial choice and the formal narrative closure of his arc, flattening the thematic weight of his death
